# Comparison with AIM 380

Target: [immutable problem statement](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/380-strong-kpp-critical-extinction.md), revision `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.

Submitted argument: [manuscript](paper/main.pdf), Theorem 1.1, Lemmas 2.1 and 3.1, and the final proof in Section 3.

The original assertion is universal over the allowed dimensions, domains and reactions. An admissible example with a positive bounded classical solution at equality is therefore a counterexample to the full assertion.

| Original requirement | Submitted witness and proof location |
| --- | --- |
| Dimension `d >= 2` | `d = 21`, Section 1, equation (3). No assertion for every dimension is needed to refute the universal implication. |
| Connected unbounded domain | Region between `z = +/- arccos(-50/(1000+|x|^2))`, Lemma 2.1. It contains the entire midplane and the straight width-pi slab. |
| Uniform `C^{2,gamma}` boundary charts | All graph derivatives are bounded, the graphs are separated, and common radius `1/4` charts have uniform bounds; Lemma 2.1. This holds for every fixed `0 < gamma <= 1`. |
| `f` in `C^{1,gamma}([0,infinity))` | Equation (4): `f(s)=s-s^2` on `[0,1]`, `f(s)=1/s-1` on `[1,infinity)`. Matching first derivatives and bounded globally Lipschitz derivative; Theorem 1.1 and its proof. |
| Zeros at 0 and 1, positive derivative at 0, prescribed signs | The same equation has `f'(0)=1`, is positive between 0 and 1 and negative above 1. |
| Strictly decreasing `f(s)/s` on `(0,1]` | Quotient `1-s` on that interval. |
| Compact-test spectral equality `lambda_1(Omega)=f'(0)` | Lemma 2.1 proves the lower bound with horizontal Hardy energy and sliced interval energy, and the upper bound with explicit compact tests in the contained slab. Both give 1. |
| Bounded positive classical solution | Lemma 3.1 gives a positive strict subsolution `v`; the final proof produces `U` with `v <= U <= 1`, interior `C^2` regularity and `-Delta U=f(U)`. |
| Pointwise zero Dirichlet values | The uniform comparison function in the last paragraph gives continuous extension by zero at every boundary point. Thus `U` lies in `C^2(Omega)` intersected with `C(closure(Omega))`. |
| No periodicity or geometric convergence assumption required | None is used as an extra hypothesis on the source target. The witness itself is explicitly defined globally. |

The violated conclusion is nonexistence of a bounded positive classical equilibrium. The construction does not establish uniqueness, an optimal dimension, a full dimension classification, or a dynamical theorem for arbitrary initial data. The manuscript credits the related Hardy-potential and nonuniform-domain constructions of Rossi and Tough and the critical question of Berestycki and Graham; no priority certificate is claimed.

This comparison is a reading map, not an independent proof audit. The complete mathematical argument is in the manuscript.

records.original_target_statement:
Fix $`N\ge2`$, $`m>2`$ and $`0<s<1`$.

On $`\mathbb R^N`$ use the model

```math
u_t=\nabla\cdot(u^{m-1}\nabla p),\qquad p=(-\Delta)^{-s}u,
```

where the inverse fractional Laplacian has Fourier multiplier $`|\xi|^{-2s}`$. Take nonzero, nonnegative $`u_0\in L^1\cap L^\infty`$ with compact support. By a bounded energy weak solution mean a nonnegative distributional solution with the initial trace $`u_0`$, continuous into $`L^1`$ with its weak topology, conserving $`\int u_0`$, and satisfying $`\|u(t)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty`$, locally integrable flux, and

```math
\frac12\|(-\Delta)^{-s/2}u(t)\|_2^2+
\int_0^t\!\int u^{m-1}|\nabla(-\Delta)^{-s}u|^2
\le\frac12\|(-\Delta)^{-s/2}u_0\|_2^2.
```

Use also the dissipative $`L^q`$ inequalities, for every $`q>1`$,

```math
\|u(t)\|_q^q+\frac{4q(q-1)}{(m+q-1)^2}\int_0^t\|(-\Delta)^{(1-s)/2}u^{(m+q-1)/2}\|_2^2\,dr\le\|u_0\|_q^q.
```

Does every bounded energy weak solution admit a representative continuous on $`\mathbb R^N\times(0,\infty)`$? Continuity must hold across the boundary of the set $`\{u>0\}`$, not merely inside that set.

# Comparison with AIM problem 467

Target: [467. Continuity for degenerate fractional-pressure porous-medium flow](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/467-fractional-pressure-superquadratic-continuity.md) at commit `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.

The original assertion is universal over its parameters, data and bounded energy weak solutions. A single admissible solution lacking the requested representative refutes that assertion. The manuscript proves a general obstruction in the strict subrange 1/2 < s < 1 and uses existing global existence to obtain the concrete witness N = 2, m = 3, s = 3/4, u₀ the indicator of the unit ball. The witness is specified by the existence theorem; an explicit formula for the solution is not claimed.

| Original requirement | Manuscript location and coverage |
| --- | --- |
| N ≥ 2, m > 2, 0 < s < 1 | Theorem 1.2 proves non-continuity for all N ≥ 2, m > 2, 1/2 < s < 1. Corollary 1.3 fixes N = 2, m = 3, s = 3/4 inside the original range. |
| Nonnegative, nonzero u₀ in L¹ ∩ L∞ with compact support | Definition 1.1 and Corollary 1.3; the fixed datum is the unit-ball indicator. |
| Distributional equation u_t = div(u^(m−1) ∇p) on R^N | Equation (1), Definition 1.1 and Appendix A use the same equation and the same global solution from the cited existence theorem. |
| p = (−Δ)^(−s) u with multiplier ∣ξ∣^(−2s) | The unitary Fourier convention in Section 1 sets I_β to multiplier ∣ξ∣^(−β), so p = I_(2s)u. |
| Initial trace u₀ | Definition 1.1 and Appendix A give the trace, including at t = 0, without restarting the solution. |
| Continuity into L¹ with its weak topology | Appendix A constructs one representative continuous against every bounded test function. |
| Conservation of mass | Definition 1.1 and Appendix A give mass M = ∫u₀ > 0 at every time. |
| Uniform bound by ∥u₀∥∞ | Definition 1.1 and Appendix A retain the source L∞ bound H. |
| Locally integrable flux | Lemma 2.2 gives the stronger bound ∣F∣ ≤ V u and global flux integrability on each finite slab, for F = −u^(m−1)∇p. |
| Pressure energy inequality with coefficient 1/2 | Equation (2), sourced from Stan–del Teso–Vázquez; Appendix A extends it to every prescribed endpoint. Initial energy finiteness is checked in the proof of Corollary 1.3. |
| Every dissipative L^q inequality, q > 1, with the original coefficient and power | Equation (3) has coefficient 4q(q−1)/(m+q−1)² and power (m+q−1)/2. Appendix A proves all endpoint inequalities for the same representative. |
| Representative continuous on R^N × (0,∞), including across vacuum | Theorem 1.2 excludes any such global jointly continuous representative. Proposition 2.3 uses continuity at vacuum in the exterior halfspaces; Section 3 obtains the dissipation contradiction. Corollary 1.3 supplies an actual solution, so the obstruction is nonvacuous. |

The contradiction uses q = 2, but the selected solution satisfies the entire required family q > 1 and the pressure energy inequality. It does not prove a classification for s ≤ 1/2, spatial discontinuity at every time, a jump profile, or a discontinuity location. The cited existence and m = 2 regularity results are attributed in the manuscript. The public original problem is used for its formulation and curation; no exhaustive novelty claim is made.

This is a complete negative-answer claim to the universal assertion, submitted for independent mathematical review. The package itself makes no catalogue classification change.

records.original_target_statement:
Fix $`n\ge2`$, $`1/2<s<1`$ and $`T>0`$. For a unit vector $`e`$ set

```math
D_e^s\phi(x)=C_s\int_0^\infty\frac{\phi(x+re)+\phi(x-re)-2\phi(x)}{r^{1+2s}}\,dr,
```

where $`C_s>0`$ is fixed. Consider $`u_t=\Delta_\infty^s u`$ on $`\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)`$ with bounded uniformly continuous initial data. Use the following viscosity convention: at a test contact with nonzero spatial gradient the right-hand side is $`D_e^s\phi`$, $`e=\nabla\phi/|\nabla\phi|`$; at a zero-gradient contact, subsolutions satisfy $`\phi_t\le\sup_{|e|=1}D_e^s\phi`$, and supersolutions satisfy $`\phi_t\ge\inf_{|e|=1}D_e^s\phi`$. In every test, patch the test function with the tested solution outside a spatial neighborhood of the contact point.

For bounded continuous viscosity sub- and supersolutions $`u,v`$, attaining their initial data uniformly, does

```math
u(\cdot,0)\le v(\cdot,0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u(x,t)\le v(x,t)\quad\text{for all }(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]?
```

No radial symmetry or monotonicity is assumed.

# Comparison with problem 042

This comparison uses the accompanying finished manuscript and the
[original public problem at its fixed revision](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/042-accurate-bidiagonal-svd.md).
The contribution is an analytic floating-arithmetic construction, accompanied
by research software and ordinary finite numerical validation.

| Original requirement | Finished manuscript | Scope and interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Real upper bidiagonal input, including signed entries | Section 2; Theorem 2.1 | The stored binary64 input is the mathematical input. Reducible, singular and repeated-value cases are included. |
| Any k distinct requested ordered ranks | Section 2 and Algorithm 1 | 1 <= k <= n; output order follows the caller's requested ranks. Repeated values allow the stated orthonormal-basis freedom. |
| Unit left and right vectors | Equation (1), Theorem 2.1 | A nonzero floating carrier x represents the exact direction x/sqrt(x^T x). This convention is explicit; the raw array is not claimed to have exactly unit norm. |
| Nonnegative estimates and ordered-value accuracy | Theorem 2.1, equation (2); Section 6 | The common error constant is 128 for represented unit directions. |
| Both singular-vector equations | Theorem 2.1, equation (3); Section 6 | Both residuals are at most 128 n epsilon \|\|B\|\|_2, including the zero-value branch. |
| Separate left and right orthogonality, independent of gaps/clusters | Theorem 2.1, equation (4); Sections 4 and 6 | Pairwise inner products are at most 128 n epsilon. The common near-zero cut handles the mixed left-direction products. |
| O(nk) arithmetic work | Algorithm 1 cost discussion; Theorem 2.1; Sections 3-6 | Fixed-format interpretation: O(p^4 nk) operations on O(p)-bit numbers, conservatively O(p^6 nk) bit work. This is O(nk) in n,k after fixing p; no precision-uniform O(nk) claim is made. |
| Small epsilon n; exclude overflow/underflow | Section 2 | epsilon=2^-p, integer 16 <= p <= 53, n epsilon <= 1/64. Correct rounding, protected exact indices and power-of-two scaling are specified. Binary64 input/output storage is fixed. |
| Actual floating arrays | Corollary 6.1 | Raw arrays satisfy value/residual/orthogonality bounds with conservative constant 256 and squared-norm defect at most 8 epsilon. This is distinct from exact unit-direction semantics. |
| Public mathematical dependencies | References [4]-[5] at their printed theorem locators | The finite-dimensional spectral theorem and Cauchy derivative estimate are used under the stated finite-dimensional/analytic hypotheses. The construction and rounding bounds are in the manuscript. |

The sufficient core precision is 67584+2880p bits, or 220224 bits at p=53.
The paper claims a fixed-format complexity construction, not practical speed
superiority. The Python/C++ implementation has finite allocation, index and
resource limits, documented separately. Its optional exact rational checker
validates an individual original input/output pair at additional cost; tests
and the two fixed matrices do not prove the universal theorem.

The claim is submitted for independent mathematical review under the explicit
arithmetic and represented-direction conventions above. No extension to
complex matrices, formal verification, independent human certification, or
repository acceptance is asserted.

records.original_target_statement:
Let $`\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d`$ be smooth, bounded and connected, $`n\ge2`$, and $`s>1`$. Set

```math
P_i(u)=u_i(a_{i0}+\sum_j a_{ij}u_j^s),\qquad
f_i(u)=b_{i0}-\sum_jb_{ij}u_j,
```

where $`a_{i0}>0`$, $`b_{i0},b_{ij}\ge0`$, and the symmetric matrix $`(a_{ij})`$ has nonnegative entries and satisfies

```math
a_{ii}>C(s)\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij},\quad
C(s)=\begin{cases}s^2/[2(s+1)(s-1)],&1<s<2,\\{[4(s-1)^2+1]}/[4(s+1)(s-1)],&s\ge2.\end{cases}
```

Choose a smooth nonnegative radial compactly supported kernel $`J`$, positive near zero, normalized by $`\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}J(z)z_1^2\,dz=1`$, and $`J_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-d}J(z/\varepsilon)`$. Let $`u^\varepsilon`$ be the global nonnegative strong solution of

```math
\partial_tu_i^\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-2}\int_\Omega J_\varepsilon(x-y)[P_i(u^\varepsilon(y))-P_i(u^\varepsilon(x))]dy+u_i^\varepsilon f_i(u^\varepsilon)
```

with fixed nonnegative $`u_i^0\in L^\infty(\Omega)\cap BV(\Omega)`$.

As $`\varepsilon\downarrow0`$, does a subsequence converge strongly in $`L^1((0,T)\times\Omega)^n`$ for every finite $`T`$ to a global weak solution of

```math
\partial_tu_i=\Delta P_i(u)+u_if_i(u),\qquad\partial_\nu P_i(u)=0,\qquad u_i(0)=u_i^0?
```

The limiting fluxes and reactions must pass to the limit in the weak formulation, not just the densities.

Locations below refer to the accompanying manuscript. This is a complete analytic solution claim awaiting independent review.

| Original requirement | Manuscript result and location | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| Every smooth bounded connected nonempty domain in dimension d >= 1; n >= 2; fixed s > 1 | Section 1.1, Theorem 1.1 | Identical |
| Positive linear diffusion; symmetric nonnegative interactions and the stated piecewise strict diagonal dominance; nonnegative reaction coefficients | Equations (1)--(2), power margin and Lemma 2.1 | Identical assumptions, no replacement by an extra condition |
| Smooth radial nonnegative compactly supported kernel, positive near zero, half-second-moment normalization | Section 1.1 and equation (3); Lemma 2.2 checks dimension one separately | Identical |
| Regional epsilon-scaled jump operator acting on the actual nonlinear pressure | Equation (4), quotient identity (25), pressure identification (28)--(29) | Identical model and normalization |
| Fixed nonnegative bounded BV data and the given global strong solutions | Section 1.1; entropy tests at fixed epsilon | Identical; strong norms are not assumed uniform in epsilon |
| Strong L1 convergence on every finite time interval | Theorem 1.1, equation (5); Lemma 3.2; final diagonal extraction | Stronger convergence in Lp for every 1 <= p < 2s, along one global subsequence |
| Pass nonlinear pressures and reactions to the local equation | Equation (6), paragraph following Lemma 3.2 | Strong L1 convergence of both actual nonlinear expressions |
| Genuine no-flux local weak solution | Equations (7)--(8); Section 3.3 | Pressure in Lr(W1r), r > 1, and arbitrary-boundary first-order tests give weak homogeneous Neumann pressure flux |

| One global weak solution and one subsequence for all finite horizons | End of Theorem 1.1 proof | Identical global quantifier |

Theorem 1.1 contains no proof-only free cutoff: the logarithmic regularization is removed at fixed epsilon, and the absorption threshold in Lemma 2.3 is fixed by the given coefficients. Constants may depend on the fixed exponent and other data. The endpoint s = 1, uniqueness, rates and convergence without subsequence are outside the claim.

The main specialized imported input is Ponce, *An estimate in the spirit of Poincare's inequality*, Theorems 1.1--1.3. Lemma 2.2 gives its exact probability-kernel normalization, L2 form-domain/mean interface, the required one-dimensional dilation condition and the fixed interval scaling. records.original_target_statement:
Let $`n\ge2`$, $`0<s<1`$, and let $`\mu`$ be a finite even nonnegative measure on $`S^{n-1}`$ such that

```math
\mu(S^{n-1})\le\Lambda,\qquad\inf_{|e|=1}\int_{S^{n-1}}|e\cdot\theta|^{2s}\,\mu(d\theta)\ge\lambda>0.
```

Define the stable operator

```math
Lu(x)=\frac12\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^\infty[2u(x)-u(x+r\theta)-u(x-r\theta)]\frac{dr}{r^{1+2s}}\,\mu(d\theta).
```

Let $`\Sigma\subsetneq\mathbb R^n`$ be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior. Suppose $`w_1,w_2`$ are continuous on $`\mathbb R^n`$, zero on $`\Sigma`$, strictly positive on $`\Sigma^c`$, and satisfy $`Lw_i=0`$ in $`\Sigma^c`$ in the viscosity sense. Assume $`|w_i(x)|\le C_i(1+|x|)^{\beta_i}`$ for some $`\beta_i<2s`$, so the tails in the equation are integrable. Must $`w_1=cw_2`$ for a constant $`c>0`$? Allow $`\mu`$ to be singular, including measures supported on finitely many directions.

| Original requirement | Manuscript location | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Every integer n >= 2 and every 0 < s < 1 | Introduction, Theorem 1.1 | Identical |
| Finite even nonnegative spectral measure, bounded total mass and positive directional 2s-moment | Equation (1.1), Theorem 1.1; class bounds (2.4)--(2.5) | Identical; singular and atomic measures are included |
| The stated positive stable operator, with factor 1/2 and the original radial normalization | Equation (1.2); measure and compensated form in Section 2 | Identical; the process generator is its negative |
| Every proper closed convex cone with nonempty interior | Theorem 1.1 | Identical |
| Globally continuous profiles, zero on the cone and positive on its complement | Theorem 1.1 | Identical |
| Harmonicity in the viscosity sense | Theorem 1.1 and Lemma 2.2 | Identical; Lemma 2.2 proves the local equivalence needed for the distributional arguments |
| Separate polynomial exponents beta_i < 2s | Theorem 1.1, Proposition 3.4 and the final proof | Identical; the temporary exponents q and p are selected inside the proof |
| A positive constant c with w_1 = c w_2 on all of R^n | Theorem 1.1 and its proof in Section 4 | Full proposed conclusion |
| No profile homogeneity or directional monotonicity assumption | Theorem 1.1; growth normalization in Proposition 3.4 | Neither is imposed |

The supporting results are stated explicitly in Lemma 2.1 and traced to Fernández-Real and Ros-Oton, *Integro-Differential Elliptic Equations*, arXiv:2411.12455v1: Lemma 2.2.30, Theorems 2.4.3, 2.4.15(b), 2.6.12, and Lemma B.1.4. Section 2 checks their general-measure applicability. The stopping argument uses the Lévy-process results identified in Schilling, arXiv:1603.00251v2, with the sign and integrability limits proved in the manuscript.

records.original_target_statement:
Let $`(M,g)`$ be a complete, connected, noncompact Riemannian manifold of dimension $`N\ge2`$, with $`\mathrm{Ric}\ge-(N-1)k`$ for some $`k\ge0`$ and the uniform Faber–Krahn inequality
$`\lambda_1(D)\ge c\,\mathrm{Vol}(D)^{-2/N}`$ for all relatively compact smooth domains $`D\subset M`$, with $`c>0`$. Fix $`m>1`$ and $`0<s<1`$ and use the spectral fractional Laplace–Beltrami operator in

```math
\partial_tu+(-\Delta_M)^s(u^m)=0.
```

For every $`o\in M`$ and $`A>0`$, does there exist a nonnegative distributional solution $`u`$ for $`t>0`$ with

```math
u\in C((0,\infty);L^1(M))\cap L^\infty_{\rm loc}((0,\infty)\times M),\qquad
0<\sup_{0<t<T}\|u(t)\|_1\le A\quad(T>0),
```

whose initial trace is $`A\delta_o`$? Precisely, require $`u^m\in L^1_{\rm loc}((0,\infty)\times M)`$, the identity

```math
\int_0^\infty\!\int_M u\,\partial_t\phi=\int_0^\infty\!\int_Mu^m(-\Delta_M)^s\phi
```

for compactly supported smooth tests (with integrable right side), and
$`\lim_{t\downarrow0}\int_Mu(t)\psi=A\psi(o)`$ for every bounded continuous $`\psi`$. No radial symmetry or homogeneity of $`M`$ is assumed.

# Comparison with AIM 474

The target is the
[original statement at revision a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/474-manifold-fractional-pme-point-source.md).
The submitted result is Theorem 1.1 of the [manuscript](paper/manuscript.pdf).
All page and equation numbers below refer to the supplied seven-page PDF.

| Original requirement | Manuscript result and location | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete, connected, noncompact Riemannian manifold; dimension N ≥ 2 | Setting on p.1 and Theorem 1.1 on p.2 | Every such manifold satisfying the two stated geometric inequalities |
| Ricci curvature bounded below by −(N−1)k for some k ≥ 0 | Equation (1), p.1; source-compatibility discussion, p.2 | Same bound; the k = 0 case is included |
| Uniform Faber–Krahn inequality for every relatively compact smooth domain, with c > 0 | Equation (1), p.1; Rayleigh-quotient argument on p.2 | The smooth-domain hypothesis suffices for the cited open-set convention |
| Every m > 1 and 0 < s < 1 | Equations (1)–(2), Theorem 1.1, pp.1–2 | Entire parameter range |
| Spectral fractional Laplace–Beltrami operator | Nonnegative Friedrichs operator L = −Δ and B = L^s, p.1; equation (14), p.4 | Same operator and sign convention |
| Every source point o and every mass A > 0 | Theorem 1.1, p.2; concentrating smooth data, p.4 | Arbitrary point and positive mass |
| Nonnegative distributional solution | Theorem 1.1; equation (3), p.1; passage to the weak equation, p.6 | Compactly supported smooth space-time tests, with the full nonlocal term |
| Strong L1 continuity at every positive time | Equation (4); global convergence (23), p.6 | One curve in C((0,∞); L1(M)) |
| Local boundedness and locally integrable u^m | Equation (4); the bound M_A(t), p.4; final passage, p.6 | Every compact subset of positive space-time |
| Integrable right side in the distributional identity | Bound on Bφ and global convergence of the powers, p.6 | Absolute integrability over all of M for each admissible test |
| 0 < sup over 0 < t < T of the L1 mass ≤ A for every T > 0 | Equation (5), p.2; closing argument, p.7 | The proof gives equality of this supremum to A; it does not require all-time mass conservation |
| Actual initial trace Aδ_o against every bounded continuous test | Equation (6); compact-test trace and final cutoff argument, p.7 | Every bounded continuous function and the actual t ↓ 0 limit |
| No radial symmetry or homogeneity | Setting and proof throughout | Neither is assumed |

Theorem 1.1 is a claim covering the complete existence target. It does not
claim uniqueness, a universal asymptotic profile, or acceptance by the
receiving repository.

## Imported results and the additional argument

The manuscript uses the bounded-data semigroup of
[Berchio–Bonforte–Grillo–Muratori, arXiv:2109.10732v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.10732v2):
Assumption 2.1 and (2.3) for the heat kernel; Proposition 5.1 and (5.5)–(5.7)
for the mild semigroup and Euler construction; Proposition 5.3 and Section 6.1
for the same solution selection; and Theorem 2.6, (2.13), for smoothing.
Lemma 2.1 states precisely the bounded-data interface used here. The
smooth-domain/open-set convention and the Ricci-bound convention are
checked on p.2 of the submitted paper.

Stochastic completeness follows from
[Grigor’yan, Theorem 15.4(a), author version pp.87–88](https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~grigor/recor.pdf).
The admissible radial comparison function is given on p.2 of the manuscript.
The Euclidean finite-measure result of
[Grillo–Muratori–Punzo, arXiv:1312.6076v3, Theorem 3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6076v3)
is cited for context and is not substituted for the manifold argument.

Sections 2–4 supply the additional bridge: the Euler energy and bounded
graph-domain test identities, heat-average tests with uniformly small
fractional generator, spatial tightness on finite horizons, compactness of
the powers, and contraction from common good times. The global L1 limit
permits the full nonlocal equation to pass to the limit. Integrability of
the nonlinear flux near time zero gives the point-mass trace. These steps
are included in the public manuscript.

OpenAI Codex assisted development and internal AI review. Independent
mathematical review is requested; no human, formal or upstream certification
is claimed.

records.original_target_statement:
Let $`(M,g)`$ be a complete, connected, noncompact Riemannian manifold of dimension $`N\ge2`$, with $`\mathrm{Ric}\ge-(N-1)k`$ for some $`k\ge0`$ and the uniform Faber–Krahn inequality
$`\lambda_1(D)\ge c\,\mathrm{Vol}(D)^{-2/N}`$ for all relatively compact smooth domains $`D\subset M`$, with $`c>0`$. Fix $`m>1`$ and $`0<s<1`$ and use the spectral fractional Laplace–Beltrami operator in

```math
\partial_tu+(-\Delta_M)^s(u^m)=0.
```

Write $`G_s(x,y)=\Gamma(s)^{-1}\int_0^\infty p_t(x,y)t^{s-1}\,dt`$, where $`p_t`$ is the heat kernel, and set

```math
\|f\|_{1,x_0,G_s}=\int_{B_1(x_0)}|f|+\int_{M\setminus B_1(x_0)}|f(x)|G_s(x,x_0).
```

All integrals use Riemannian volume. A nonnegative weak dual solution has $`u\in C([0,T];L^1_{x_0,G_s})`$ for every $`x_0,T`$, $`u^m\in L^1((0,T);L^1_{\rm loc}(M))`$, and

```math
\int_0^T\!\int_M\bigl[(-\Delta_M)^{-s}u\,\partial_t\psi-u^m\psi\bigr]=0
```

for every compactly supported smooth space-time test function $`\psi`$.

For every $`u_0\ge0`$ in $`L^1(M)`$ and every such weak dual solution with $`u(0)=u_0`$ and $`u(t)\in L^1(M)`$, prove or disprove

```math
\int_M u(t,x)\,d\mathrm{Vol}(x)=\int_Mu_0(x)\,d\mathrm{Vol}(x)\qquad(t>0).
```

This asks for conservation at every finite time, not merely the known upper bound on the total mass.

# Target comparison for AIM 473

Target: [473. Mass conservation for fractional porous-medium flow on noncompact manifolds](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/473-manifold-fractional-pme-mass-conservation.md), revision `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.

Submitted argument: [manuscript](paper/mass_conservation.pdf), Theorem 2.2. The table is based on the manuscript and the public target.

| Original requirement | Manuscript location | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Every complete connected noncompact Riemannian manifold of dimension at least two | Section 2, geometric assumptions (2), and Theorem 2.2 | Same class; no model-space or symmetry restriction |
| Ricci curvature bounded below for any nonnegative comparison constant | Assumptions (2); cutoff specialization in Lemma 2.3 | Includes zero comparison constant |
| Uniform Faber–Krahn inequality on relatively compact smooth domains | Opening of Section 2 | The variational argument proves the all-open version needed by the cited linear estimates, with the original constant and dimension |
| Every porous-medium exponent greater than one and fractional order strictly between zero and one | Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.2; interpolation in Proposition 4.1 | Entire stated ranges |
| Spectral fractional Laplace–Beltrami operator and the normalized Green kernel | Section 2, (4), normalization paragraph and Lemma 2.3 | Exact spectral realization and Gamma normalization |
| Every nonnegative integrable initial datum | Theorem 2.2; finite regularized energy in Proposition 4.1 | No boundedness or finite initial energy premise |
| Weighted continuity at every basepoint and every finite horizon | Definition 2.1; potential estimate (6) and Proposition 3.2 | Same continuity topology |
| Local time-space integrability of the nonlinear power, compact smooth dual tests and the prescribed initial trace | Definition 2.1 and (5); endpoint integration in Proposition 3.2 | No constant or nonlinear weak test is inserted |
| Every such WDS with spatial L1 membership at each finite time | Theorem 2.2 and Proposition 3.2 | A uniform mass upper bound and power integrability are derived for the given solution |
| Conservation at every finite positive time | Final proof of Theorem 2.2; all-endpoint identity (13) | Equality at every finite time, with the initial mass recovered by strong L1 continuity |

No minimality, nonlinear semigroup construction, energy-solution property or uniqueness identification is imposed on the given solution. The paper does not prove uniqueness in the larger weighted class.

The additional argument establishes the needed global nonlinear integrability for the arbitrary WDS. It is not a restatement of the constructed-solution smoothing theorem.

| Public source | Exact input used | Manuscript treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Berchio–Bonforte–Grillo–Muratori, arXiv:2109.10732v2; final Math. Ann. 389 (2024), 3603–3651 | Gaussian bound (2.3), Remark 2.1 and Lemma 5.2; linear subordination discussion in the proof of Proposition 5.1 | Section 2 states the bounds, reconciles the printed Green normalization, and proves the exact spectral potential representation |
| von Criegern–Grillo–Monticelli, arXiv:2609.12954v1 (2026), Corollary 8.6 | Conservation for WDSs constructed by monotone approximation on nonnegative-Ricci manifolds with a finite fractional Green kernel | Credited in the Introduction as a related prior result; no construction assumption is transferred to the present arbitrary WDS |
| Bianchi–Setti, arXiv:1607.06008v1, Corollary 2.3 | Ordinary Laplacian cutoffs under the Ricci lower bound | Lemma 2.3 uses their curvature exponent zero to prove heat conservativeness |
| Sard, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 48 (1942), Theorem 7.2 | Smooth scalar maps admit regular values | Section 2 constructs intermediate smooth domains for the variational FK argument |
| Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 2009 edition, Section 3.1 | Spectral functional calculus | Lemma 2.3 checks the normalized Green/semigroup representation |

The contribution is analytic. No numerical, computer-assisted or formal-proof certificate is asserted. The package is submitted for independent review; catalogue classification is left to the maintainers.

```math
\partial_t^{\alpha_1}u_1=\Delta u_1+u_1+u_2,\qquad \partial_t^{\alpha_2}u_2=\Delta u_2+u_1+u_2,
```

```math
\|U(t)\|\le C\|U_0\|^{1-t/T}\|U(T)\|^{t/T}\qquad(0<t<T)
```

for every mild solution?

# Comparison with problem 042

This comparison uses the accompanying finished manuscript and the
[original public problem at its fixed revision](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/042-accurate-bidiagonal-svd.md).
The contribution is an analytic floating-arithmetic construction, accompanied
by research software and ordinary finite numerical validation.

| Original requirement | Finished manuscript | Scope and interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Real upper bidiagonal input, including signed entries | Section 2; Theorem 2.1 | The stored binary64 input is the mathematical input. Reducible, singular and repeated-value cases are included. |
| Any k distinct requested ordered ranks | Section 2 and Algorithm 1 | 1 <= k <= n; output order follows the caller's requested ranks. Repeated values allow the stated orthonormal-basis freedom. |
| Unit left and right vectors | Equation (1), Theorem 2.1 | A nonzero floating carrier x represents the exact direction x/sqrt(x^T x). This convention is explicit; the raw array is not claimed to have exactly unit norm. |
| Nonnegative estimates and ordered-value accuracy | Theorem 2.1, equation (2); Section 6 | The common error constant is 128 for represented unit directions. |
| Both singular-vector equations | Theorem 2.1, equation (3); Section 6 | Both residuals are at most 128 n epsilon \|\|B\|\|_2, including the zero-value branch. |
| Separate left and right orthogonality, independent of gaps/clusters | Theorem 2.1, equation (4); Sections 4 and 6 | Pairwise inner products are at most 128 n epsilon. The common near-zero cut handles the mixed left-direction products. |
| O(nk) arithmetic work | Algorithm 1 cost discussion; Theorem 2.1; Sections 3-6 | Fixed-format interpretation: O(p^4 nk) operations on O(p)-bit numbers, conservatively O(p^6 nk) bit work. This is O(nk) in n,k after fixing p; no precision-uniform O(nk) claim is made. |
| Small epsilon n; exclude overflow/underflow | Section 2 | epsilon=2^-p, integer 16 <= p <= 53, n epsilon <= 1/64. Correct rounding, protected exact indices and power-of-two scaling are specified. Binary64 input/output storage is fixed. |
| Actual floating arrays | Corollary 6.1 | Raw arrays satisfy value/residual/orthogonality bounds with conservative constant 256 and squared-norm defect at most 8 epsilon. This is distinct from exact unit-direction semantics. |
| Public mathematical dependencies | References [4]-[5] at their printed theorem locators | The finite-dimensional spectral theorem and Cauchy derivative estimate are used under the stated finite-dimensional/analytic hypotheses. The construction and rounding bounds are in the manuscript. |

The sufficient core precision is 67584+2880p bits, or 220224 bits at p=53.
The paper claims a fixed-format complexity construction, not practical speed
superiority. The Python/C++ implementation has finite allocation, index and
resource limits, documented separately. Its optional exact rational checker
validates an individual original input/output pair at additional cost; tests
and the two fixed matrices do not prove the universal theorem.

The claim is submitted for independent mathematical review under the explicit
arithmetic and represented-direction conventions above. No extension to
complex matrices, formal verification, independent human certification, or
repository acceptance is asserted.

records.pr_title: 042: proposed fixed-format selected bidiagonal SVD construction
records.original_target_statement:
Let $`B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}`$ be upper bidiagonal, with singular values $`\sigma_1(B)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n(B)\ge0`$. Given $`k`$ distinct requested indices $`j_1,\ldots,j_k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}`$, construct a floating-point algorithm that computes corresponding singular triplets $`(\widehat\sigma_i,\widehat u_i,\widehat v_i)`$ in $`O(kn)`$ arithmetic operations, with unit vectors, nonnegative estimates, and

```math
|\widehat\sigma_i-\sigma_{j_i}(B)|\le C\epsilon n\|B\|_2,
```



```math
\|B\widehat v_i-\widehat\sigma_i\widehat u_i\|_2\le C\epsilon n\|B\|_2,
```



```math
\|B^T\widehat u_i-\widehat\sigma_i\widehat v_i\|_2\le C\epsilon n\|B\|_2,
```



```math
|\widehat u_i^T\widehat u_j|\le C\epsilon n,\qquad
|\widehat v_i^T\widehat v_j|\le C\epsilon n\quad(i\ne j).
```

Here $`\epsilon`$ is unit roundoff and $`C`$ is a universal constant, independent of singular-value gaps or clusters; assume $`\epsilon n`$ is small and exclude overflow and underflow. A repeated value permits any orthonormal basis of its singular subspace.

# Comparison with problem 042

This comparison uses the accompanying finished manuscript and the
[original public problem at its fixed revision](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/042-accurate-bidiagonal-svd.md).
The contribution is an analytic floating-arithmetic construction, accompanied
by research software and ordinary finite numerical validation.

| Original requirement | Finished manuscript | Scope and interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Real upper bidiagonal input, including signed entries | Section 2; Theorem 2.1 | The stored binary64 input is the mathematical input. Reducible, singular and repeated-value cases are included. |
| Any k distinct requested ordered ranks | Section 2 and Algorithm 1 | 1 <= k <= n; output order follows the caller's requested ranks. Repeated values allow the stated orthonormal-basis freedom. |
| Unit left and right vectors | Equation (1), Theorem 2.1 | A nonzero floating carrier x represents the exact direction x/sqrt(x^T x). This convention is explicit; the raw array is not claimed to have exactly unit norm. |
| Nonnegative estimates and ordered-value accuracy | Theorem 2.1, equation (2); Section 6 | The common error constant is 128 for represented unit directions. |
| Both singular-vector equations | Theorem 2.1, equation (3); Section 6 | Both residuals are at most 128 n epsilon \|\|B\|\|_2, including the zero-value branch. |
| Separate left and right orthogonality, independent of gaps/clusters | Theorem 2.1, equation (4); Sections 4 and 6 | Pairwise inner products are at most 128 n epsilon. The common near-zero cut handles the mixed left-direction products. |
| O(nk) arithmetic work | Algorithm 1 cost discussion; Theorem 2.1; Sections 3-6 | Fixed-format interpretation: O(p^4 nk) operations on O(p)-bit numbers, conservatively O(p^6 nk) bit work. This is O(nk) in n,k after fixing p; no precision-uniform O(nk) claim is made. |
| Small epsilon n; exclude overflow/underflow | Section 2 | epsilon=2^-p, integer 16 <= p <= 53, n epsilon <= 1/64. Correct rounding, protected exact indices and power-of-two scaling are specified. Binary64 input/output storage is fixed. |
| Actual floating arrays | Corollary 6.1 | Raw arrays satisfy value/residual/orthogonality bounds with conservative constant 256 and squared-norm defect at most 8 epsilon. This is distinct from exact unit-direction semantics. |
| Public mathematical dependencies | References [4]-[5] at their printed theorem locators | The finite-dimensional spectral theorem and Cauchy derivative estimate are used under the stated finite-dimensional/analytic hypotheses. The construction and rounding bounds are in the manuscript. |

The sufficient core precision is 67584+2880p bits, or 220224 bits at p=53.
The paper claims a fixed-format complexity construction, not practical speed
superiority. The Python/C++ implementation has finite allocation, index and
resource limits, documented separately. Its optional exact rational checker
validates an individual original input/output pair at additional cost; tests
and the two fixed matrices do not prove the universal theorem.

The claim is submitted for independent mathematical review under the explicit
arithmetic and represented-direction conventions above. No extension to
complex matrices, formal verification, independent human certification, or
repository acceptance is asserted.

records.original_target_statement:
Let $`X,U`$ be Banach spaces, let $`A`$ generate a strongly continuous semigroup $`S(t)`$ on $`X`$, and let $`X_{-1}`$ be the completion of $`X`$ for the norm $`\|x\|_{-1}=\|(\lambda-A)^{-1}x\|_X`$, where $`\lambda`$ belongs to the resolvent set of $`A`$. Denote the extended semigroup by $`S_{-1}`$ and fix $`B\in\mathcal L(U,X_{-1})`$. Assume $`L^\infty`$-admissibility: for every $`T>0`$, there is $`K_T<\infty`$ such that for every strongly measurable $`u\in L^\infty(0,T;U)`$,

```math
\Phi_Tu:=\int_0^T S_{-1}(T-s)Bu(s)\,ds\in X,\qquad \|\Phi_Tu\|_X\le K_T\|u\|_{L^\infty}.
```

Must $`t\mapsto\int_0^t S_{-1}(t-s)Bu(s)\,ds`$ be continuous from $`[0,T]`$ to $`X`$ for every such input and every $`T>0`$?

# AIM 411: comparison with the full original target

Target:
[Continuity of states driven by bounded admissible inputs](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/411-bounded-input-state-continuity.md),
revision `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.
The [manuscript](paper/continuity.pdf) contains the entire submitted proof.

| Original requirement | Manuscript location and result | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arbitrary Banach state and input spaces `X,U` | Section 1, Theorem 1; both real and complex fields are included | Full; no geometric or separability assumption |
| `A` generates a strongly continuous semigroup | Section 1 retains the original generator and semigroup | Identical |
| Resolvent-norm completion `X_{-1}` and compatible extended semigroup | Section 1 defines the same completion and the canonical injection and extended resolvent | Identical |
| Bounded `B:U -> X_{-1}` | Section 1, equation (1) | Identical |
| Every finite horizon and every strongly measurable essentially bounded input | Equation (1) explicitly quantifies over the original input class | Full |
| Endpoint in `X` with a bound independent of the input | Equation (1), with `K_T` depending on the system and horizon | Identical admissibility assumption |
| Original Bochner convolution state at each time | Theorem 1 states exactly that convolution and assigns zero at time zero | Identical |
| Norm continuity on the whole closed interval | Theorem 1 and the last part of its proof in Section 3 | Full, including time zero and the terminal left limit |
| No additional space geometry or input regularity | Lemma 2 constructs a separable state subspace separately for each fixed input; the pasted input in Section 3 is strongly measurable and bounded | No added hypothesis |
| Stronger conclusion, not an extra premise | Equation (3) proves uniform decay of the full control operator norm on the input unit ball | Zero-class admissibility; no quantitative rate claimed |

The two central intermediate results are Lemma 2 (actual state-norm separable
range and weak compactness of a fixed-input scalar multiplier) and Lemma 3
(norm countable additivity). Section 3 supplies the disjoint-interval
contradiction and the fixed-earlier-state continuity argument.

The imported scalar Grothendieck mapping result is
González--Kania, arXiv:2102.03838v3, Theorem 3.1.1 and Proposition 4.1.5.
The Orlicz--Pettis and Pettis measurability theorems are in Diestel,
*Sequences and Series in Banach Spaces*, Chapter IV, pages 24--25.
The extrapolation conventions are those of Weiss (1989), Definition 3.1,
Proposition 3.3 and Remark 3.4. Their hypotheses and uses are stated in the
manuscript. Preußler--Schwenninger, arXiv:2605.12121v1, Corollary 4.10 and
the discussion after Corollary 4.11 supply the cited geometric prior cases.

The submission covers the entire represented-convolution problem printed
in AIM 411. The original axiomatic formulation of Weiss's question can be
broader; no claim about input maps lacking the stated `B`-convolution
representation is made. This comparison records a complete solution claim,
not human peer review, formal verification or upstream acceptance.

records.original_target_statement:
Let $`\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d`$, $`d\ge2`$, be bounded with smooth boundary, and let $`N\ge2`$, $`d_i>0`$. Let $`f:[0,\infty)^N\to\mathbb R^N`$ be locally Lipschitz, with $`f_i(z)\ge0`$ when $`z_i=0`$, and suppose some $`\mu\in\mathbb R^N`$ satisfies

```math
\sum_i f_i(z)(\log z_i+\mu_i)\le0\qquad(z_i>0).
```

No growth bound on $`f`$ is imposed. For nonnegative $`u_0`$ with $`\sum_i\int_\Omega u_{i,0}(1+|\log u_{i,0}|)<\infty`$, is the renormalized solution of

```math
\partial_tu_i=d_i\Delta u_i+f_i(u),\qquad\partial_\nu u_i=0,\qquad u_i(0)=u_{i,0},
```

unique?

Precisely, the comparison class consists of nonnegative $`u_i\in L^\infty(0,T;L^1)`$, $`\sqrt{u_i}\in L^2(0,T;H^1)`$ for every $`T<\infty`$, such that for each smooth $`\xi:[0,\infty)^N\to\mathbb R`$ with compactly supported $`D\xi`$, each smooth $`\psi`$ on $`\overline\Omega\times[0,T]`$, and almost every $`T`$,

```math
\begin{aligned}
\int_\Omega\xi(u(T))\psi(T)-\int_\Omega\xi(u_0)\psi(0)-\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\xi(u)\partial_t\psi
={}&-\sum_{i,j}d_i\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\psi\xi_{ij}(u)\nabla u_i\cdot\nabla u_j\\
&-\sum_i d_i\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\xi_i(u)\nabla u_i\cdot\nabla\psi
+\sum_i\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\xi_i(u)f_i(u)\psi .
\end{aligned}
```

Products of gradients are interpreted using $`\nabla u_i=2\sqrt{u_i}\nabla\sqrt{u_i}`$; the cutoff makes all displayed terms integrable. The question is equality almost everywhere of any two such solutions with the same initial data, without assuming that a bounded strong solution exists.

records.original_target_statement:
Let $`N:\mathbb R^2\to[0,\infty)`$ be a norm, smooth away from zero, with positive-definite Hessian of $`N^2`$ there. Put $`K=\{v:N(v)\leq1\}`$ and parametrize $`\partial K`$ by $`N`$-arclength $`\gamma(s)`$. The billiard map on ordered distinct boundary points is generated by $`L(s,t)=N(\gamma(t)-\gamma(s))`$: successive parameters satisfy

```math
\partial_2L(s_{j-1},s_j)+\partial_1L(s_j,s_{j+1})=0.
```

If its entire phase annulus is foliated by continuous invariant simple curves winding once around the annulus, must $`N(v)=\sqrt{v^TQv}`$ for a positive-definite symmetric matrix $`Q`$?

# Comparison with Problem 252

Target: [Rigidity of a totally integrable Minkowski billiard in its own unit ball](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/252-self-ball-minkowski-integrability.md), repository revision `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.

Submitted claim: Theorem 1.1 in [the manuscript](paper/minkowski_integrability.pdf). It proves the entire stated implication for the original smooth strongly convex class.

| Original requirement | Manuscript location and agreement |
|---|---|
| Every norm on the real plane, smooth off zero with positive-definite Hessian of its square | Section 1 defines exactly this class; Theorem 1.1 quantifies over every such norm. Section 2 uses its strong convexity for positive curvature, twist and a nondegenerate support maximum. |
| Table is the norm's own unit ball | Section 1 sets K={N<=1}; Section 2 sets P=-J K*, so the propagation norm and table are linked exactly as in the problem. |
| Boundary parametrized by N-arclength and chord generating function N(gamma(t)-gamma(s)) | Both definitions and the Euler--Lagrange equation appear in Section 1. Section 2.1 explains why smooth boundary reparametrization preserves the finite stationary Hessian. |
| Entire phase annulus | Total integrability is defined for the entire ordered-distinct-point annulus. Section 2.2 covers every original orbit and both alternating phase components; Section 2.3 averages the whole union. |
| Continuous invariant simple curves winding once | Section 1 uses precisely this C0 hypothesis. Section 2.1 imports the continuous-invariant-curve local maximum property; no differentiability of leaves is assumed. |
| Positive-definite symmetric Q with N(v)=sqrt(v^T Qv) for all v | Theorem 1.1 states this conclusion. Its final proof forces equality in the polar area-product bound, obtains a centered ellipse, and identifies its gauge, including at zero. |
| No extra symmetry or self-polarity assumption | Only central symmetry supplied by the norm is used. Section 2.3 uses antipodes; Section 2.2 permits the position and momentum curves to be different. |

The main supporting steps are Lemma 2.1 (support maximum), Sections 2.1--2.3 (negative finite variations, complete half maps, invariant measure and averaging), Lemma 3.1 (boundary parameter and polar area product), and Lemma 3.2 (energy determinant bound). These steps are proved in the public manuscript.

External inputs are identified where used: Bialy's general positive-mixed-derivative twist statement for continuous essential invariant curves, Bianchi--Kelly's symmetric Blaschke--Santalo inequality and equality case, and ordinary planar isoperimetry as presented by Osserman. The prior finite-linear-symmetry theorem and neighboring single symplectic-table rigidity theorem are credited as context; neither is asserted to cover the full target directly.

The paper makes a complete analytic solution claim. It asserts neither upstream acceptance nor a formal verification result. Integrability only near the boundary of phase space is outside the theorem.

records.pr_title: 485: proposed optimal obstacle regularity for integrable angular densities
records.original_target_statement:
Let $`n\ge2`$, $`0<s<1`$, and $`0<\lambda\le\Lambda`$. Let $`a\in L^1(\mathbb S^{n-1})`$ be nonnegative and even, with

```math
\int_{\mathbb S^{n-1}}a(\theta)\,d\theta\le\Lambda,\qquad \inf_{e\in\mathbb S^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb S^{n-1}}|e\cdot\theta|^2a(\theta)\,d\theta\ge\lambda.
```

Set $`K(y)=a(y/|y|)|y|^{-n-2s}`$ and

```math
\mathcal E_a(w)=\frac14\int_{\mathbb R^n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|w(x)-w(x+y)|^2K(y)\,dy\,dx.
```

For any nonnegative $`\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)`$, let $`u`$ be the unique minimizer of $`\mathcal E_a`$ over

```math
\{w\in L^{2n/(n-2s)}(\mathbb R^n):\mathcal E_a(w)<\infty,\ w\ge\phi\text{ almost everywhere}\}.
```

This is the finite-energy obstacle solution associated with $`Lu=\mathop{\mathrm{p.v.}}\nolimits\int(u(x)-u(x+y))K(y)\,dy`$. Does a constant $`C=C(n,s,\lambda,\Lambda)`$ always exist such that

```math
\|u\|_{C^{1,s}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\phi\|_{C^3(\mathbb R^n)}?
```

Here the left side is $`\|u\|_\infty+\|\nabla u\|_\infty+\sup_{x\ne y}|\nabla u(x)-\nabla u(y)|/|x-y|^s`$. There is no assumption that $`a`$ belongs to any $`L^p`$ with $`p>1`$, or that the kernel is positive in every direction.

# Comparison with AIM 485

Original target: [Optimal obstacle regularity for stable jump kernels with only angular integrability](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/485-general-stable-obstacle-optimal-regularity.md), revision `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.

Submitted claim: Theorem 1.1 of [the manuscript](paper/main.pdf). All locations below refer to this manuscript. The original target prescribes its unique finite-energy minimizer. Theorem 1.1 is an a priori estimate for every minimizer in exactly that class; Lemma 4.1 also shows uniqueness through the energy zero-space argument. No additional regularity of the minimizer is assumed.

| Original requirement | Manuscript location and argument | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every n >= 2 and 0 < s < 1 | Theorem 1.1; Section 2 fixes precisely these ranges | Full |
| Nonnegative even a in L1 on the sphere; total mass <= Lambda | Equation (1.1) and Theorem 1.1; Section 2 identifies the density operator with the spectral formula | Full |
| Every quadratic directional moment >= lambda | Equation (1.1); Section 2 computes the general elliptic-class constants, and Appendix A derives directional cap mass | Full |
| Every nonnegative phi in C_c^infinity | Theorem 1.1 and Section 4 | Full |
| The prescribed energy and L^{2n/(n-2s)} finite-energy minimizer | Equations (1.2)--(1.3); Section 4 proves comparisons with admissible positive-part tests in that same homogeneous class | Full |
| Positive principal-value operator and its normalization | Introduction and equation (2.2); Section 4 uses energy = B(u,u)/2 | Full |
| Uniform full global C^{1,s} norm | Theorem 1.1; Proposition 4.3 gives separation from contact, and the closing proof covers all gradient pairs and the two supremum norms | Full |
| Constants only C(n,s,lambda,Lambda), without obstacle support radius | Theorem 1.1; compactness over the mass/moment class in Sections 2--3; fixed normalizations and support-independent forcing bound in Section 4 | Full |
| No stronger angular Lp assumption or positivity in every direction | Theorem 1.1; Appendix A uses cap mass and total mass, and Proposition 4.2 invokes only the density mass/moment flatness result | Full |

## Public inputs

The bibliography gives exact public source versions. The linear estimates, maximum principle, Liouville theorem and stable barrier come from Fernandez-Real and Ros-Oton, arXiv:2411.12455v1, Theorem 2.4.3, Lemma 2.3.5, Theorem 2.4.15(b), Corollary 2.4.14 and Lemma 2.6.2. The ball Hopf bound uses Grube, arXiv:2410.00829v1, Proposition 1.7(3) and Proposition 6.7; a smooth tangent ball and global nonnegativity satisfy its geometric and exterior assumptions. The half-line uniqueness input is Grube and Ros-Oton, arXiv:2605.18711v1, Theorem 1.1. The final flatness input is Ros-Oton and Weidner, arXiv:2308.01695v1, Proposition 5.8, applied only to angular densities. Its small forcing gradient, semiconvexity, actual free-boundary point, growth and Lipschitz profile approximation are checked in Section 4.

The necessary additional argument is the convex-primitive cone rigidity in Proposition 3.1, followed by the classification and radius-normalized approximation in Section 3. Appendix A supplies measure-uniform compactness instead of assuming that a density theorem automatically holds for singular measures.

## Scope and evidence

This is a complete analytic claim for the density-class target above. The auxiliary classification permits singular spectral measures, but the endpoint obstacle estimate for all such measures is not asserted. There are no numerical or computer-assisted proof claims. No separate detailed AI review is submitted; independent mathematical review is requested.

records.pr_title: AIM 455: deterministic Hölder exponent for smooth transport SPDEs
records.original_target_statement:
On $`\mathbb T^d`$, $`d\ge2`$, consider the scalar Itô equation

```math
du=\nabla\cdot(a\nabla u)\,dt+\sum_{k\ge1}(b_k\cdot\nabla u)\,dW^k_t,\qquad u(0)=u_0,
```

where the Brownian motions are independent, $`u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^d)`$ is deterministic, and the coefficients are progressively measurable in $`(t,\omega)`$ and measurable in $`x`$. Assume fixed deterministic bounds

```math
|a|+\Big(\sum_k|b_k|^2\Big)^{1/2}\le M,\qquad
\eta^\top\Big(a-\tfrac12\sum_kb_k\otimes b_k\Big)\eta\ge\nu|\eta|^2\quad(\eta\in\mathbb R^d),
```

with $`M<\infty`$ and $`\nu>0`$. Use the variational solution in $`C([0,T];L^2)\cap L^2(0,T;H^1)`$, defined by testing against smooth spatial functions and integrating the stochastic terms in the Itô sense.

Now assume that $`b=(b_k)_k`$ is smooth in $`x`$ and, for every integer $`j\ge1`$, obeys a deterministic uniform bound $`\sup_{t,\omega}\|b(t,\omega,\cdot)\|_{C^j(\mathbb T^d;\ell^2(\mathbb R^d))}\le M_j`$. The diffusion matrix $`a`$ remains merely bounded and measurable. For every $`0<\tau<T`$, is there a deterministic $`\gamma>0`$, depending only on $`d,\nu,M,(M_j),\tau,T`$, such that

```math
\mathbb P\bigl(u\in C^{\gamma/2,\gamma}([\tau,T]\times\mathbb T^d)\bigr)=1?
```

The Hölder norm itself may be random and unbounded. The question is whether the exponent can be chosen independently of the sample; no commuting-flow or spatially constant-noise assumption is allowed.

# Comparison with problem 042

This comparison uses the accompanying finished manuscript and the
[original public problem at its fixed revision](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/042-accurate-bidiagonal-svd.md).
The contribution is an analytic floating-arithmetic construction, accompanied
by research software and ordinary finite numerical validation.

| Original requirement | Finished manuscript | Scope and interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Real upper bidiagonal input, including signed entries | Section 2; Theorem 2.1 | The stored binary64 input is the mathematical input. Reducible, singular and repeated-value cases are included. |
| Any k distinct requested ordered ranks | Section 2 and Algorithm 1 | 1 <= k <= n; output order follows the caller's requested ranks. Repeated values allow the stated orthonormal-basis freedom. |
| Unit left and right vectors | Equation (1), Theorem 2.1 | A nonzero floating carrier x represents the exact direction x/sqrt(x^T x). This convention is explicit; the raw array is not claimed to have exactly unit norm. |
| Nonnegative estimates and ordered-value accuracy | Theorem 2.1, equation (2); Section 6 | The common error constant is 128 for represented unit directions. |
| Both singular-vector equations | Theorem 2.1, equation (3); Section 6 | Both residuals are at most 128 n epsilon \|\|B\|\|_2, including the zero-value branch. |
| Separate left and right orthogonality, independent of gaps/clusters | Theorem 2.1, equation (4); Sections 4 and 6 | Pairwise inner products are at most 128 n epsilon. The common near-zero cut handles the mixed left-direction products. |
| O(nk) arithmetic work | Algorithm 1 cost discussion; Theorem 2.1; Sections 3-6 | Fixed-format interpretation: O(p^4 nk) operations on O(p)-bit numbers, conservatively O(p^6 nk) bit work. This is O(nk) in n,k after fixing p; no precision-uniform O(nk) claim is made. |
| Small epsilon n; exclude overflow/underflow | Section 2 | epsilon=2^-p, integer 16 <= p <= 53, n epsilon <= 1/64. Correct rounding, protected exact indices and power-of-two scaling are specified. Binary64 input/output storage is fixed. |
| Actual floating arrays | Corollary 6.1 | Raw arrays satisfy value/residual/orthogonality bounds with conservative constant 256 and squared-norm defect at most 8 epsilon. This is distinct from exact unit-direction semantics. |
| Public mathematical dependencies | References [4]-[5] at their printed theorem locators | The finite-dimensional spectral theorem and Cauchy derivative estimate are used under the stated finite-dimensional/analytic hypotheses. The construction and rounding bounds are in the manuscript. |

The sufficient core precision is 67584+2880p bits, or 220224 bits at p=53.
The paper claims a fixed-format complexity construction, not practical speed
superiority. The Python/C++ implementation has finite allocation, index and
resource limits, documented separately. Its optional exact rational checker
validates an individual original input/output pair at additional cost; tests
and the two fixed matrices do not prove the universal theorem.

The claim is submitted for independent mathematical review under the explicit
arithmetic and represented-direction conventions above. No extension to
complex matrices, formal verification, independent human certification, or
repository acceptance is asserted.

On $`\mathbb R^3`$, let $`\nu>0`$ and let $`b_1,\ldots,b_K\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)`$ be divergence-free, with

```math
\nu I-\tfrac12\sum_k b_k(x)\otimes b_k(x)\ge\delta I\quad(\delta>0).
```

Write $`\mathbb P`$ for the Helmholtz projection onto divergence-free fields. Is the Itô equation

```math
du=[\nu\Delta u-\mathbb P\nabla\cdot(u\otimes u)]dt+\sum_k\mathbb P[(b_k\cdot\nabla)u]dW^k_t
```

locally well posed for every deterministic divergence-free $`u_0\in B^{-1/2}_{6,4}(\mathbb R^3)`$? More precisely, does it admit a positive stopping time $`\tau`$ and an adapted mild solution with

```math
u\in C([0,\tau];B^{-1/2}_{6,4})\cap L^4(0,\tau;L^6)\quad\hbox{almost surely},
```

pathwise uniqueness in this class, and continuous dependence in probability in these norms after stopping on common local intervals? The mild equation uses the heat semigroup for both the drift and stochastic convolution. The initial Besov space is the usual inhomogeneous Littlewood–Paley space. The assertion must cover all such spatially varying transport fields, with no extra smallness assumption.

| Heat semigroup in drift and stochastic mild convolutions | Equation (1.3) is the required identity. Section 2.3 verifies strong/mild agreement and the continuous convolution versions. |
| Positive stopping time and adapted local solution | Section 3.2 constructs the progressive truncated solution and a strictly positive stopping time (3.5); the cutoff is one throughout that stopped interval. |
| C([0,tau];B^{-1/2}_{6,4}) intersect L^4(0,tau;L^6), almost surely | Theorem 1.1 states exactly these spaces; Lemma 2.1, (2.11) and Section 3.2 supply the trace and time norm. |
| Pathwise uniqueness in this entire class | Section 3.3 compares arbitrary solutions with only almost-sure norms, on bounded-norm random slabs. No fourth-probability-moment assumption is added to the solution class. |
| Initial-data continuity in probability in both norms on common local intervals | Theorem 1.1 and Section 3.4 give both-norm convergence after stopping on tau_n wedge tau. They also give rho>0 with P(tau_n<rho) tending to zero, so the common intervals are nondegenerate. |
| No extra smallness assumption | Section 3.2 chooses a cutoff radius from finite coefficient-dependent constants and works on the whole process Banach space for arbitrary data. The radius is a proof choice, not a condition on the initial velocity or fields. |

The manuscript claims the complete written target above. It does not claim
global well-posedness, an optimal critical data class, or an independent proof
of the external linear maximal-regularity theorem. That published theorem and
its localized interface are stated and cited explicitly in Proposition 2.2.
Independent mathematical review of this solution claim is requested.

records.original_target_statement:
On $`\mathbb T^2`$, set $`\Lambda=(-\Delta)^{1/2}`$ and $`R^\perp=(-R_2,R_1)`$, with zero Fourier multiplier at frequency zero. Consider

```math
d\theta+[R^\perp\theta\cdot\nabla\theta+\Lambda\theta]dt
=\sum_{k=1}^K g_k(x,\theta)\,dW^k_t,\qquad\theta(0)=\theta_0,
```

in the Itô sense. The initial temperature $`\theta_0`$ is any deterministic smooth periodic function. The finite collection $`g_k`$ consists of smooth functions on $`\mathbb T^2\times\mathbb R`$, globally Lipschitz in their scalar argument uniformly in $`x`$, with bounded derivatives of positive order and bounded $`g_k(\cdot,0)`$. The $`W^k`$ are independent standard Brownian motions.

Does every such equation have a pathwise unique global adapted solution with paths in $`C([0,T];H^3(\mathbb T^2))`$ for every finite $`T`$, satisfying the integral equation in $`H^1`$? Equivalently, can its local $`H^3`$ solution blow up with positive probability? No smallness of the data or noise is imposed, and the $`g_k`$ need not be linear in $`\theta`$.

# Target comparison for Problem 478

The target is [Problem 478: Global regularity for critical SQG with state-dependent noise](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/478-critical-stochastic-sqg-global-regularity.md), at revision `a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22`.
The result claimed in the accompanying manuscript is Theorem 1.1.

| Original requirement | Manuscript result and location | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Critical Ito SQG on the two-dimensional torus, Lambda=(-Delta)^(1/2), Riesz multipliers zero on constants | Equation (1.1), conventions at the end of Section 1, and the full-space realization (2.1) | Same equation and normalization. The constant mode is retained. |
| Every deterministic smooth periodic datum | Assumptions before Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 2.1 | Entire stated datum class; no smallness or zero-mean condition. |
| Every finite smooth coefficient family, globally scalar-Lipschitz uniformly in space, bounded positive-order derivatives and bounded g_k(x,0) | Equation (1.2), Theorem 1.1, local composition estimate (2.3), noise increment estimate (4.2), and tame estimate (4.12) | Full stated spatial/state-dependent nonlinear class. No affine or additive restriction. |
| Prescribed independent Brownian motions and adapted pathwise solution | Theorem 1.1, Proposition 2.1, and final proof in Section 4.4 | Same stochastic basis and Brownian motions; no replacement noise. |
| Almost-sure global existence for every finite horizon | Proposition 3.1, Proposition 4.2, estimate (4.13), and Section 4.4 | Finite maximal lifetime is excluded by countable deterministic localization. |
| Pathwise uniqueness and paths continuous in H3 | Theorem 1.1 and the last paragraph of its proof | Both are global on every finite time interval. |
| Integral identity in H1 | Theorem 1.1 and the final paragraph in Section 4.4 | The proof obtains the identity in H2, which implies the requested H1 identity. |

The amplitude estimate is proved before amplitude localization. At each fixed integer amplitude level, a spatial exponent is chosen independently of the finite power used in the increment integral; a sufficiently large finite power gives a positive Holder exponent. The final countable exhaustion removes these auxiliary stopping levels without adding a hypothesis.

The manuscript uses the local theorem of Roeckner--Zhu--Zhu through an explicit realization on full L2, the periodic spatial kernel estimates of Constantin--Tarfulea--Vicol, and the continuous martingale estimate and iteration method of Hsu--Wang--Wang. Their roles and applicable formulas are stated and the remaining argument is given in the paper. It does not invoke a previously proved global nonlinear critical endpoint theorem.

This is a complete solution claim for the displayed original target, submitted for independent mathematical review. Catalogue classification and acceptance remain with the maintainers.

records.original_target_statement:
Fix $`d\ge2`$ and $`\chi>0`$. For every compactly supported $`\rho_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^d)`$ with $`\rho_0\ge0`$ and $`\int\rho_0=1`$, does

```math
\partial_t\rho=-\nabla\cdot(\rho\nabla\Delta\rho)-\chi\Delta(\rho^2),\qquad \rho(0)=\rho_0,
```

admit a nonnegative global weak solution with the following finite-propagation property: for every $`T<\infty`$, some $`R_T<\infty`$ satisfies $`\rho(t,x)=0`$ for almost every $`(t,x)\in(0,T)\times(\mathbb R^d\setminus B_{R_T})`$?

Here a weak solution is a narrowly continuous probability-valued curve with finite second moment and

```math
\rho\in L^\infty(0,T;H^1)\cap L^2(0,T;H^2)
```

for every finite $`T`$, satisfying, for all $`\phi\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^d)`$ and $`0\le a<b`$,

```math
\int\phi[\rho(b)-\rho(a)]=-\int_a^b\!\int\bigl(\rho\Delta\rho\Delta\phi+\Delta\rho\nabla\rho\cdot\nabla\phi+\chi\rho^2\Delta\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt.
```

Narrow continuity means continuity against bounded continuous spatial tests. Only existence of a solution preserving bounded support on finite time intervals is requested; weak uniqueness is a separate question.

# Comparison with the original AIM 481 target

Source: [original problem at the fixed repository revision](https://github.com/MColbrook/AIM/blob/a153f469ee0ea64e876b2ad97c79d252c19a3e22/problems/481-fourth-order-aggregation-finite-propagation.md). The submitted result is Theorem 1.1 of the [finished manuscript](paper/main.pdf), with proof in Sections 2–4 and Appendix A.

| Original requirement | Submitted statement and argument |
| --- | --- |
| Every integer $`d\ge2`$ and every $`\chi>0`$ | Theorem 1.1 has exactly these ranges. The small entropy exponent depends on $`d`$ and remains strictly within the finite-exponent Sobolev range. |
| Every compactly supported, nonnegative $`\rho_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^d)`$ with mass one | Exactly the datum class in Theorem 1.1. Positive floors and smoothness occur only in an auxiliary construction and are removed. |
| A nonnegative global, narrowly continuous probability-valued curve with finite second moment and the prescribed initial value | Theorem 1.1 and the original minimizing movement construction in Section 2.1. A common global subsequence is retained. |
| $`L^\infty(0,T;H^1)\cap L^2(0,T;H^2)`$ on every finite horizon | Stated in Theorem 1.1; the construction bounds are displayed in (2.3)–(2.4). |
| The exact weak identity for every compact $`C^2`$ test and every pair of time endpoints | Equation (1.2), with the same sign, coefficient $`\chi`$ and three integrands as the problem. |
| One finite radius for almost every point of the entire spacetime interval $`(0,T)`$ | Theorem 1.1; the local entropy bound (4.1) and the superlinear tail recurrence (4.8) force the exterior spacetime tail to be zero beyond a finite radius. |
| The same curve for all finite horizons | The fixed countable cutoff family and integer-horizon argument at the end of Section 4. |

The equation is

```math
\partial_t\rho=-\nabla\cdot(\rho\nabla\Delta\rho)-\chi\Delta(\rho^2).
```

For every $`\phi\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^d)`$ and $`0\le a<b`$, the submitted identity is

```math
\int\phi[\rho(b)-\rho(a)]
=-\int_a^b\!\int\bigl(\rho\Delta\rho\Delta\phi+\Delta\rho\nabla\rho\cdot\nabla\phi+\chi\rho^2\Delta\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt.
```

The comparison uses the problem's explicit Sobolev requirements. Definition 2.1(i) of the pinned CEFF preprint also writes a spatial infinity endpoint in dimension two. The manuscript distinguishes that extra wording and uses the common $`H^1/H^2`$ estimates and their finite-exponent consequences; no spatial infinity endpoint is claimed. This omits no clause of the AIM statement above.

The submission does not assert weak uniqueness, a quantitative radius law, or a conclusion for every possible weak solution. It presents a full-target solution claim for independent mathematical review. AI assistance and the actual review limits are disclosed in [AI_USE.md](AI_USE.md); no human, Lean, novelty or repository-acceptance certificate is asserted.
